newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-Grim life in cages for poorest in HK.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Grim life in cages for poorest in HK.

text.p: An old man lay in a rectangular cage of wire-mesh, staring into space. Sharing his "cage home" were all his worldly possessions, in flimsy plastic bags.

Below him was an identical cage-home with its own array of bags hanging about the wire mesh. But this one, with wet laundry strung inside, was padlocked. His neighbour was out, said grey-haired Chu Pak-fatt, 74.
Looking at Chu and the other 39 cages -- double-decked and lined in tight columns in a cramped, filthy, all-male apartment -- it was hard to believe they were in affluent Hong Kong.
The cages, smaller than you would expect to find for an animal in a zoo, allow the occupant only to sit up or lie down.
The "Pearl of the Orient" boasts a per capita income of HK$193,000 (US$25,000), among the world's highest, but the cage-life of the poorest is a horrifying sight by any standard.

"What is there to hope for the future? I only hope to save a little. Anyway, I am over 70 years old. I don't have much hope," said Chu, a retired tailor, who has slept in the very same cage for the last 40 years. "I only wish to die early."

With more Rolls-Royces per head than anywhere else in the world, "one in every ten people in Hong Kong is living under the poverty line," Chua Hoi-wai, a researcher with the Hong Kong Council of Social Services, said in a recent interview.
In actual numbers, between 600,000 and 800,000 people in Hong Kong's 6.4 million population are estimated to live on or below the poverty line, Chua said.

The Hong Kong Social Security Society found in a survey late last year that the top 10 percent of households in Hong Kong shared 42 percent of gross income while the bottom 50 percent had only 19 percent of wealth.
FROM CAGE TO COFFIN-LIKE BOX
A tailor for 50 years, Chu was forced to retire after he was knocked down by a bus during a visit in China three years ago.

Chu now receives HK$1,900 per month in social security but spends at least half of that on medical bills. The government pays HK$500 per month to his landlord for his rented cage -- which measures an even more dismal 1.75 metres (5.75 ft) length by 0.75 metres (2.46 ft) breadth by 0.80 metres (2.6 ft) height.
"I just have to eat less, each month I spend about HK$1,000 to pay for Chinese medicine. My bills at government hospitals are paid for by the government," he said.
At the other end of the apartment, a group of sweaty, bare-chested mainland Chinese workers cooked dinner in a kitchen near a squalid toilet.

Two blocks from the decrepit and rubbish-strewn pre-World War Two building housing Chu and his fellow "cagemen" in Sham Shui Po, one of Hong Kong's densest housing estates, was another type of living arrangement for the poor -- windowless boxes.
"Their situation is even worse, they sleep in tiny bedspaces completely boarded up by wooden planks. They are like coffins," said Iman Fok, a social worker.
"It's so hot I sleep with the door open, it's so terrible here. Even though the government pays the rent, I am still human," said unemployed Tang Fong-cheung, 59.
Tang's home, a cage like Chu's but boarded up by thin wooden planks instead of wire-mesh, has no window.
BUT THEY HOLD THEIR HEADS HIGH
Despite their plight, many of Hong Kong's poor are proud and would rather suffer than take payouts from welfare authorities.
"Our social workers encourage poor people to apply for social security but many would rather suffer," researcher Chua said. "They feel relying on the government is a shameful thing."
Of at least 640,000 people living in poverty, only 150,000 receive any kind of welfare.

Those who are recipients are apologetic and many do not ask for more. "It's hard to ask for more from the government. They have already paid for my medical fees, if I see a Chinese doctor, it's my own fault," said cageman Chu.
The world's leading importer of Cognac and one of the highest per capita users of cellular phones, Hong Kong has no official definition of poverty.
"But when we say poverty we roughly mean people who don't have enough income to support their own housing and food needs," Chua said.
Spiralling housing costs and an influx of mainland Chinese willing to take jobs at low wages in the last 10 years have displaced low-skilled Hong Kong people, Chua said.

Hong Kong, a British run-colony for over 150 years, returns to China at midnight this June 30, and Chua fears the problem may worsen if more Chinese secure "one-way" permits to settle here. (US$1 = HK$7.72)
